lineages.name: Kraftwerk
lineages.why: They treated their Kling Klang studio as an instrument and built their own tools: a vocoder, an electronic drum kit with sensor pads, and the Synthanorma sequencer (1976). From Autobahn to Computer World, their minimal, repetitive 'robot pop' set the template for synth-pop.

lineages.name: Martin Rushent with The Human League
lineages.why: On Dare, Rushent layered as many as 24 analogue synths on a line, programmed a guide beat on the Linn and added fills afterwards, and comped Phil Oakey's vocals from three takes. He kept a bass line's accidental half-beat slip. 'Don't You Want Me' went to number one in the UK and the US.

lineages.name: Vince Clarke
lineages.why: He writes by imagining a part and programming it, since he says he is not a good enough keyboard player to write on the synth. He programmed the Roland MC-4 by entering numbers for CV, gate and control data, and his favourite synths are the Pro One, System-100M, System 700 and Juno-60.

lineages.name: New Order
lineages.why: For 'Blue Monday' Bernard Sumner had a sequencer built to sync a DMX and a Moog Source before MIDI existed. Gillian Gilbert wrote the part by hand and kept her accidental extra rest, and an Emulator sampled the choir from Kraftwerk's 'Uranium'.

name: Synth-pop / EDM pop

notes.text: Synthesizers, drum machines and sequencers, sometimes replacing every other instrument. Early work is minimalist, repeated melodic elements without complex harmonic development, and acts often worked as duos: a singer and a programmer.

On Dare, Martin Rushent layered synths heavily, sometimes 24 on one line, 'all drifting out of tune', to make the sound full. The Linn LM-1 laid a rudimentary guide beat, with every fill programmed afterwards.

Sequencers drive the groove. Vince Clarke ran several synths from a Roland MC-4 CV/gate sequencer, entering CV, gate and control data as numbers, and says the revolution in electronic music came with the sequencer, not with any synth.

'Blue Monday' ran an Oberheim DMX and a Moog Source bass from a sequencer the band built before MIDI. Gillian Gilbert wrote the sequence by hand, and an extra rest she put in by accident was kept as part of the song's feel.
The bass is a sequenced synth line locked to the machine, such as the Moog Source on 'Blue Monday' or the Roland on the 'Don't You Want Me' chorus, whose half-beat timing slip Rushent kept.

Modal minor loops with bright turns are common. 'Blinding Lights' cycles i-v-bVII-IV in F Dorian; 'Don't You Want Me' has its verse in A minor and its chorus in the relative C major; 'Take On Me' uses seventh chords (ii7-V7-I-IV7-iii7) and a Phrygian-coloured bridge.

Verse-chorus form with a bridge before the final chorus. Intros have shrunk from over 20 seconds in the mid-1980s to about 5 seconds, and in 2014 the first chorus arrived at 0:33 on average, with only 5% after a minute.

Rushent and Jo Callis tracked drums, bass and vocals first, then added synth lines, horns playing pad chords on the chorus, and strings for commercial lift, and softened the originally harsher synth score.
The singer carries the human part. 'Take On Me' spans A2 to a falsetto E5, over two and a half octaves, and is called one of the hardest choruses in pop to sing; that is the extreme, not the norm.
Emotional, even operatic, lead vocals (Marc Almond, Alison Moyet, Annie Lennox) against cool machines. 'Don't You Want Me' was reworked from a male solo into a 'conflicting duet'.
Phil Oakey's vocals were comped from three takes and recorded in a tiled bathroom for its live reflections; Susan Sulley's verse took about 60 takes.

Judge loudness by era. In lufs.to's sample the median is -16.7 LUFS for the 1980s, -12.0 for the 1990s, -10.6 for the 2000s and -9.4 for the 2010s. Current pop releases have a median of -9.5 (middle half -11.2 to -8.1).

evidence.inferred: computed by Bench/genres/melody_ranges.py over https://colinraffel.com/projects/lmd/ and https://www.tagtraum.com/msd_genre_datasets.html

notes.text: Melody ranges are measured, not recalled: 637 eight-bar windows from the melody tracks of 117 Lakh MIDI files labelled Electronic by tagtraum, each read with the app's own Melodist arithmetic; the range is the 10th to 90th percentile, typical the median. Performed MIDI, so note lengths are as played. The share of chord tones is not measured: the files carry no chords. The label is the Million Song Dataset's Electronic label, measured only where a MIDI file has a melody or vocal track, which is mostly vocal dance-pop and synth-pop.

pitfalls.text: One clean synth on each line sounds thin and cold. Layer and detune: Rushent stacked many analogue synths on one line and let them drift.

Quantising every accident away. Several of the genre's defining feels were mistakes that were kept: Gilbert's extra rest in 'Blue Monday' and the half-beat slip of the bass on the 'Don't You Want Me' chorus.

Expecting the machines to write the song. OMD's Andy McCluskey answered the 'soulless' critique by pointing out that synthesizers do not make hits by themselves; the melody and the singer still have to.
A 1980s-length instrumental intro on a modern single. Intros have fallen from over 20 seconds to about 5, and most hits reach the first chorus by 0:40.

progressions.text: Blinding Lights, verse and chorus in F Dorian: the major IV is the Dorian colour, and the loop never cadences.
Don't You Want Me's pre-chorus in A minor, which hands over to a chorus in C major.
Take On Me's verse: a ii-V-I with seventh chords, unusually jazzy for the style.
Take On Me's chorus: the axis progression under the falsetto climb.

summary: Pop songs played on synthesizers, drum machines and sequencers, which often replace every other instrument. The parts are often minimal repeated figures, and the singers are frequently emotional, even operatic. It runs from Kraftwerk and the British early-1980s charts (Human League, Depeche Mode, New Order) to the 21st-century revival that produced 'Blinding Lights'.
